questions.stem: Which is a testable hypothesis for an investigation of a swinging pendulum?
options: If the pendulum's length increases, its period will increase
Pendulums are interesting to watch because they swing back and forth
The pendulum will swing in a way that depends on several factors
Investigating a pendulum will help us understand how pendulums work
questions.explanation: A testable hypothesis predicts how a dependent variable (the period) will respond to a change in an independent variable (the length), so an experiment can support or refute it. The other statements make no measurable prediction.

questions.stem: A student hypothesises that a heavier pendulum bob gives a longer period. Her results show the same period for every mass she tests. What should she do next?
options: Keep the hypothesis, because a hypothesis based on scientific knowledge cannot be wrong
Leave out the lightest and heaviest masses, because they are the results that disagree
Modify the hypothesis to fit the evidence: the period may not depend on the mass
Repeat the experiment until the results show that heavier bobs give a longer period after all
questions.explanation: Hypotheses are revised in response to evidence. Her data does not support the original prediction, so she should modify it and test the new version. Repeating until the expected result appears, or discarding inconvenient data, is poor and unethical practice.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the angle of a ramp affects the acceleration of a trolley rolling down it. Which correctly identifies the variables?
options: Independent: acceleration; dependent: ramp angle; controlled: trolley mass and ramp surface
Independent: trolley mass; dependent: acceleration; controlled: ramp angle and ramp surface
Independent: ramp angle; dependent: trolley mass; controlled: acceleration and ramp surface
Independent: ramp angle; dependent: acceleration; controlled: trolley mass and ramp surface
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the student changes on purpose (the angle), and the dependent variable is the one measured in response (the acceleration). Everything else that could affect the acceleration, such as the trolley's mass and the surface, must be kept constant.

questions.stem: In an investigation of how an iron core affects an electromagnet, a student also tests the same coil with no core at all. What is the purpose of this coil with no core?
options: It is an experimental control, a baseline to compare each core against
It is the independent variable, because the core is what the student is changing
It is a controlled variable, because it keeps the current through the coil constant
It is an outlier, because it gives a much weaker field than all the other trials
questions.explanation: An experimental control is a set-up in which the factor being tested is absent, giving a baseline to compare against. Without it, the student could not tell how much of the field is due to the core rather than the coil alone. A controlled variable, by contrast, is a quantity kept constant in every trial.

questions.stem: To test how the length of a wire affects its resistance, a student uses a longer, thinner wire for each trial. Why is the investigation invalid?
options: Resistance cannot be measured accurately for thin wires, so the results will not be precise
The investigation does not have enough repeat trials, so the results will not be reliable
Length and resistance are both scalars, so a graph of one against the other is meaningless
Length and thickness both change, so the effect of length alone cannot be found
questions.explanation: A valid investigation tests only what it claims to test, changing one independent variable while controlling all others. Here the cross-sectional area changes along with the length, so any change in resistance cannot be attributed to length alone.

questions.stem: How can a student make the primary data in an investigation more reliable?
options: Change several variables at once, so that more effects are tested in each trial
Round all the measurements to fewer significant figures so that they agree
Repeat each measurement several times and check that the results are consistent
Use only one carefully taken measurement, to avoid confusing different readings
questions.explanation: Reliability is about consistency: repeat trials that give similar results show the data can be trusted, and averaging them reduces the effect of random error. A single measurement gives no way of telling how consistent results would be.

questions.stem: A student wants secondary data on the refractive index of a type of glass. Which source would be most reliable?
options: A peer-reviewed physics data handbook whose value agrees with other reputable sources
A personal blog that quotes a value without giving any source for it at all
A forum post with a value that many users have liked and shared
An advertisement from a glass company stating that its product is the best
questions.explanation: Secondary data is more reliable when it comes from authoritative, peer-reviewed sources and agrees with other independent reputable sources. Popularity does not make data accurate, and an advertisement may be biased.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a hazard from a risk when planning an investigation?
options: A hazard is how likely the harm is to happen; a risk is the possible source of the harm
A hazard is harm that has already happened; a risk is harm that could happen in future
A hazard is a minor danger; a risk is a serious danger that needs a written plan
A hazard is a possible source of harm; a risk is how likely and severe that harm is
questions.explanation: A hazard is anything that could cause harm, such as a laser beam. The risk depends on how likely the harm is and how bad it would be. A risk assessment identifies hazards, judges the risks and sets out controls to reduce them.

questions.stem: Students use a laser to investigate refraction through a glass block. Which control measure best reduces the main risk?
options: Wear thick gloves when handling the glass block to protect against the laser
Work in a darkened room so the laser beam is easier to see when it reflects
Shine the laser through a water tank first so that it loses most of its energy
Use a low-power laser, keep the beam below eye level and never look along it
questions.explanation: The main hazard of a laser is eye damage from the direct or reflected beam. Using a low-power laser, keeping the beam horizontal below eye level and never looking into it reduces both the likelihood and the severity of harm. Gloves do not protect the eyes.

questions.stem: Why do school circuit experiments use low-voltage power packs rather than mains electricity?
options: Mains electricity cannot be measured with ammeters and voltmeters
Low-voltage supplies are the only ones that obey Ohm's law
Low voltages greatly reduce the risk of a dangerous electric shock
Low voltages make the current flow in the opposite direction
questions.explanation: The severity of an electric shock depends on the current through the body, which a higher voltage drives more readily. Low-voltage supplies greatly reduce this hazard, making the experiment safer without changing the physics being studied.

questions.stem: A student finds that one trial disagrees with her predicted result, so she leaves it out of her report without mentioning it. Why is this an ethical problem?
options: Every trial must always be included, even if a clear mistake was made in taking it
Data that disagrees with a prediction is always the most accurate data in the set
Results must be reported honestly; data may be excluded only with a stated reason
Only teachers are allowed to remove results from a student's report, never the student
questions.explanation: Scientific integrity requires honest reporting. A result may be excluded, for instance a clear outlier caused by a known mistake, but the exclusion and its reason must be stated so others can judge it. Quietly removing inconvenient data misrepresents the evidence.

questions.stem: A group measures g four times and gets 9.51, 9.53, 9.52 and 9.52 m s⁻². The accepted value is 9.8 m s⁻². How would you describe these results?
options: Accurate but not precise, suggesting a random error
Both accurate and precise, so there is no error present
Neither accurate nor precise, suggesting a random error
Precise but not accurate, suggesting a systematic error
questions.explanation: The results are very close to one another, so they are precise, but all are about 0.3 m s⁻² below the accepted value, so they are not accurate. A consistent offset like this points to a systematic error, such as friction or a timing delay, which repetition cannot remove.

questions.stem: An ammeter reads 0.02 A when no current is flowing. What kind of error does this cause, and how is it dealt with?
options: A systematic zero error, reduced by repeating every reading and averaging the results
A random error, corrected by subtracting 0.02 A from every reading
A systematic zero error, corrected by subtracting 0.02 A from every reading
A random error, reduced by repeating every reading and averaging the results
questions.explanation: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, so it is systematic and affects accuracy. Averaging repeats does not remove it, because every reading is offset equally; it must be corrected, by zeroing the meter or subtracting the offset.

questions.stem: Which statement about random and systematic errors is correct?
options: Repeating and averaging increases random error but reduces systematic error
Repeating and averaging reduces random error but does not reduce systematic error
Repeating and averaging reduces systematic error but does not reduce random error
Repeating and averaging reduces both random error and systematic error equally
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter readings above and below the true value, so they partly cancel when averaged. A systematic error shifts all readings the same way, so averaging leaves it unchanged; it must be found and corrected or the method improved.

questions.stem: A graph of voltage against current for a resistor gives a straight line with a positive gradient that cuts the voltage axis at +0.30 V instead of passing through the origin. What does this suggest?
options: The resistance is 0.30 Ω, read from the intercept
A systematic error, such as a zero error in the voltmeter
A random error, caused by reading the voltmeter carelessly
The resistor is non-ohmic, because the line is straight
questions.explanation: Theory predicts V = IR, a line through the origin. A straight line shifted up by the same amount at every point means every voltage reading is offset by about 0.30 V, the signature of a systematic error such as a zero error. The resistance is still the gradient, which the offset does not change.

questions.stem: The period of a pendulum is measured four times: 2.04 s, 2.10 s, 1.98 s and 2.08 s. What are the mean and the range?
options: Mean 2.05 s, range 0.12 s
Mean 2.05 s, range 0.06 s
Mean 2.06 s, range 0.12 s
Mean 2.04 s, range 0.10 s
questions.explanation: The mean is (2.04 + 2.10 + 1.98 + 2.08)/4 = 8.20/4 = 2.05 s. The range is the largest minus the smallest value: 2.10 − 1.98 = 0.12 s.

questions.stem: What does the standard deviation of a set of repeated measurements show?
options: The difference between the largest and smallest values
The number of measurements that were outliers
How widely the measurements are spread about their mean
How far the mean is from the accepted value
questions.explanation: The standard deviation measures the spread of data about the mean: a small standard deviation means the readings are close together, so the data is precise. How far the mean is from the accepted value describes accuracy, measured by percentage error.

questions.stem: Two groups measure the speed of sound. Group 1's results have a mean of 341 m s⁻¹ with a standard deviation of 2 m s⁻¹. Group 2's have a mean of 343 m s⁻¹ with a standard deviation of 9 m s⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
options: Group 2's results are more precise, because their mean is closer to the accepted value
Group 1's results are more accurate, because their standard deviation is smaller
Both sets are equally precise, because their means differ by only 2 m s⁻¹
Group 1's results are more precise, because their spread about the mean is smaller
questions.explanation: Precision describes how closely repeated results agree, which the standard deviation measures; Group 1's smaller standard deviation shows greater precision. Accuracy describes closeness to the accepted value, a different property that the standard deviation does not measure.

questions.stem: A student measures the speed of sound as 330 m s⁻¹. The accepted value is 343 m s⁻¹. What is the percentage error?
questions.explanation: Percentage error = |330 − 343|/343 × 100 ≈ 3.8%. Dividing by the measured value instead gives 3.9%, and 96% is the measured value as a percentage of the accepted value.

questions.stem: A length is measured with a ruler marked in millimetres. What is the usual absolute uncertainty of a single reading?
options: ±1 mm
±5 mm
questions.explanation: The absolute uncertainty of an analogue scale is usually taken as half the smallest division, so ±0.5 mm for a ruler marked in millimetres.

questions.stem: A length is recorded as 25.0 ± 0.5 cm. What is its percentage uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty = absolute uncertainty/measured value × 100 = 0.5/25.0 × 100 = 2%. Writing the fraction 0.02 as if it were already a percentage gives 0.02%.

questions.stem: A student times 10 complete swings of a pendulum as 15.0 s, with an uncertainty of ±0.2 s from reaction time. What is the period with its absolute uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Dividing both the time and its uncertainty by 10 gives T = 1.50 ± 0.02 s. The reaction-time uncertainty is the same however many swings are timed, so timing many swings shrinks the uncertainty in each period. Leaving the uncertainty as ±0.2 s ignores this benefit.

questions.stem: A student records the times for a trolley to roll down a ramp as 1.52 s, 1.49 s, 1.51 s, 1.89 s and 1.50 s. How should the 1.89 s result be treated?
options: As an outlier: look for a cause, repeat the trial, and note any exclusion from the mean
As the most accurate value, since it is the furthest from the others and must be carefully measured
As part of the mean like every other value, since no result may ever be excluded for any reason
As proof the ramp angle changed during the trials, so all five results should be thrown away
questions.explanation: The 1.89 s value lies far from the others and is an outlier, probably from a mistake such as a late start. It should be investigated and the trial repeated; if it is excluded from the mean, the report should say so and why. Including it would distort the mean.

questions.stem: A theory predicts that y is inversely proportional to x. Which graph should give a straight line through the origin?
options: y against x
y against x²
1/y against 1/x
y against 1/x
questions.explanation: If y = k/x, then y = k(1/x), so plotting y against 1/x gives a straight line through the origin with gradient k. Plotting y against x gives a curve (a hyperbola), which makes the relationship hard to confirm.

questions.stem: To find a trolley's mass from its kinetic energy, a student plots kinetic energy against v². What does the gradient of the straight line represent?
options: The mass, m
Twice the mass, 2m
The speed, v
Half the mass, m/2
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv², so a graph of KE against v² is a straight line through the origin with gradient ½m. The mass is twice the gradient. Plotting against v² rather than v is what makes the graph linear.

questions.stem: For a simple pendulum, T = 2π√(L/g). A graph of T² against L is a straight line with a gradient of 4.0 s² m⁻¹. What value of g does this give?
options: 4.0 m s⁻²
2.5 m s⁻²
9.9 m s⁻²
questions.explanation: Squaring gives T² = (4π²/g)L, so the gradient is 4π²/g and g = 4π²/4.0 ≈ 9.9 m s⁻². Taking the gradient itself as g gives 4.0, its reciprocal gives 0.25, and treating the gradient as 2π/√g gives 2.5.

questions.stem: Data is collected on how the speed of a trolley (a continuous variable) depends on the height of a ramp (also continuous). Which representation is most suitable?
options: A table only, because graphs hide the trend
A scatter graph with a line or curve of best fit
A column graph with one column for each height
A pie chart showing the share of each speed
questions.explanation: When both variables are continuous, a scatter graph with a line or curve of best fit shows the relationship and lets values be read between the data points. Column graphs suit categories, such as different materials, and pie charts show parts of a whole.

questions.stem: A student's data on the extension of a material under load fits a straight line for loads up to 5.0 N. She uses the line to predict the extension at 20 N. Why is this prediction unreliable?
options: Predictions from graphs are never valid in physics unless they agree with a textbook
It is an extrapolation well beyond the data, where the relationship may no longer hold
It is an interpolation within the data, where the relationship is known not to hold
Straight-line graphs can only be used for predictions when they pass through the origin
questions.explanation: Reading a value within the range of the data (interpolation) is reasonable, but extending the line far beyond it (extrapolation) assumes the relationship continues, which may not be true. Many materials stop behaving linearly at larger loads.

questions.stem: How many significant figures does the measurement 0.004050 m have?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only place the decimal point and are not significant. The digits 4, 0, 5 and the final 0 are significant, because a trailing zero after the decimal point shows the precision of the measurement. That is 4 significant figures.

questions.stem: A trolley travels 12.5 m in 4.0 s. How should its average speed be recorded?
options: 3 m s⁻¹
3.1 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: 12.5/4.0 = 3.125, but a result should have no more significant figures than the least precise measurement used. The time, 4.0 s, has two significant figures, so the speed is 3.1 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: What is 250 nm expressed in metres?
questions.explanation: Nano means 10⁻⁹, so 250 nm = 250 × 10⁻⁹ m = 2.50 × 10⁻⁷ m. Writing 2.50 × 10⁻⁹ m forgets that 250 is not between 1 and 10.

questions.stem: Which conversion between a prefixed unit and powers of ten is correct?
questions.explanation: Giga means 10⁹, so 3.2 GHz = 3.2 × 10⁹ Hz. Pico is 10⁻¹² (not 10⁻⁹, which is nano), mega is 10⁶ (not 10³, which is kilo), and micro is 10⁻⁶ (not 10⁻³, which is milli).

questions.stem: The radius of an atomic nucleus is a few femtometres. What power of ten does the prefix femto represent?
options: 10¹⁵
10⁻¹⁵
10⁻¹²
questions.explanation: Femto (f) is 10⁻¹⁵, so 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m. Pico is 10⁻¹² and nano is 10⁻⁹; 10¹⁵ is peta.

questions.stem: A car travels at 72 km h⁻¹. What is this speed in m s⁻¹?
options: 20 m s⁻¹
260 m s⁻¹
1.2 m s⁻¹
7.2 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 000 m/3600 s = 20 m s⁻¹; dividing by 3.6 converts km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹. Multiplying by 3.6 gives about 260, and dividing by 60 gives 1.2.

questions.stem: A wire has a cross-sectional area of 5.0 mm². What is this area in square metres?
questions.explanation: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, so 1 mm² = (10⁻³)² m² = 10⁻⁶ m², and 5.0 mm² = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Using 10⁻³ forgets to square the conversion factor along with the unit.

questions.stem: A student times a falling ball with a hand-held stopwatch and gets widely scattered results. Which change would most improve the reliability and accuracy of the timing?
options: Use a heavier ball so that it falls through the air faster
Record the times to more decimal places on the stopwatch
Drop the ball from a lower height so it is easier to see
Use light gates connected to a data logger to time the fall
questions.explanation: Human reaction time is the main source of error with a stopwatch. Light gates and a data logger time the fall automatically, removing both the scatter and the delay. Recording more decimal places does not make a reaction-limited measurement more accurate.

questions.stem: Light is often modelled as rays travelling in straight lines. What is a limitation of this ray model?
options: It has no limitations, because it is the true description of how light behaves
It cannot explain diffraction and interference, which need a wave model of light
It cannot explain reflection from a plane mirror, which needs a particle model of light
It cannot explain refraction at a boundary, which needs a model of light as sound
questions.explanation: Models are simplified representations that work within limits. The ray model handles reflection and refraction well, but cannot account for light spreading through narrow gaps or forming interference patterns; for those, a wave model is needed.

questions.stem: Newton's laws of motion were later found to fail at speeds close to the speed of light and were extended by Einstein's relativity. What does this show about scientific knowledge?
options: It is testable and contestable, so it can be refined when new evidence is found
It is fixed once published, so older theories must be discarded completely
It depends on the opinion of the most famous scientists of the time
It cannot be tested, so theories are replaced whenever fashions change
questions.explanation: Scientific ideas are tested against evidence and can be challenged and refined. Newton's laws still work extremely well at everyday speeds; relativity extends physics to situations where they fail. Theories change because of evidence, not opinion or fashion.

questions.stem: Before a physics research paper is published in a journal, it usually goes through peer review. What does this involve?
options: Scientists repeat their own experiments to check that the results are reliable
Independent experts check the study's methods, data and conclusions
Students compare their answers with each other before handing in a report to their teacher
The public votes on whether new scientific findings should be accepted
questions.explanation: In peer review, other experts in the field scrutinise a study's methods, analysis and conclusions before publication, helping to catch errors and unsupported claims. Repeating your own experiment improves reliability but is not peer review.
